item.title: Surgical Skill Prediction from Behavioral Patterns
item.description: This project analyzed the behavioral patterns of different subject groups (students, residents, attendings) doing a surgical simulation task. 2D hand pose estimations were estimated from multiple views and triangulated to 3D hand pose sequences. A monocular body pose estimation model was applied to estimate the subject’s body pose movement during the task session. Analyses on the estimated pose sequences reveal significant differences between students and experienced doctors.

item.title: Detecting Behavioral Signatures within DeepFake videos
item.description:
Generated motion-transferred DeepFake videos with state-of-the-art lipsyncing and face reenactment models to investigate the behavioral signatures (speaking style and utterance, etc.) in person identification. User Study reveals that the behavioral signatures significantly affect the user identification of the person.

item.title: Multi-person Multi-view Close Proximity Estimation
item.description: This project analyzes close proximity from videos captured from different views when multiple children were participating in group activities. We calculated the fundamental matrix from the keypoint matchings across views. Then we performed cross-view matching for the same person using the appearance features and geometry correlations between the keypoints, including epipolar and homography. A state-of-the-art person re-identification model was fine-tuned on this data to track the same person across the time frame. After extracting the keypoints and bounding boxes for all target persons, we built and trained a Siamese Multi Layer Perceptron (MLP) to regress the close proximity scores for each person in each minute. The model is able to regress reasonable close proximity estimations even given very unbalanced and noisy labels.

item.title: Brain Neural Mechanisms when Objects are Masked in Scenes
item.description: This project investigated the brain neural mechanisms in human scene categorization when the “signature objects” were masked. We collected functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data of subjects doing a scene categorization task when signature objects were visible or masked, and conducted statistical analyses to investigate the changes in neural activations, functional connectivities, and activation patterns. The results reveal the role of object and scene-selective regions, especially the top-down modulation effect from the fronto-parietal regions in object-based scene categorization.
